chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all from Ibn Mahboub, from Ibn Raib, from Abu Ubayda, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The slave, when he flees from his masters, then steals, his hand is not cut while he is a fugitive because he is a renegade from Islam, but he is called to return to his masters and enter into Islam. If he refuses to return to his masters, his hand is cut due to the theft, then he is killed; and the apostate, when he steals, is treated at his status.

key_terms.إِبَاق: Fleeing of a slave from his master

ai.seo_question: What is the penalty for a fleeing slave who steals according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the jurisprudential status of an 'abiq' (fugitive slave) who is deemed a renegade (murtadd) from Islam, thereby suspending the hadd penalty for theft until he is summoned to return to his master and re-enter the faith. If he refuses, the hand is cut for theft followed by execution, illustrating the Shia scholarly view that apostasy and servitude intersect to delay corporal punishment until the spiritual status is resolved. This ruling underscores the practical implication that the 'abiq' is not merely a criminal but a spiritual defector, with the apostate's theft penalty remaining consistent with this dual status.
